issues.subcategory: Inconsistent sample size across reporting
issues.description: The final sample size is reported as N = 372 in the Methods, but both Table 1 and Table 2 report N = 321, and Table 3 reports N = 244. The discrepancy between the stated final sample (372) and the analytic sample (321) is never explained. This undermines confidence in the analyses and prevents replication. Where did the additional 51 participants go between the sample-construction description and the actual analyses?
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.subcategory: Attrition arithmetic does not add up
issues.description: The retention figures and exclusion counts are mutually inconsistent. The authors state n = 450 responded at T4, then say only those completing all four surveys were included with n = 16 excluded for missing time points and n = 78 for data quality, which would yield roughly 450 - 78 = 372 (the stated final N), but the exclusion of 16 for missing time points contradicts the claim that non-responders were not invited to later waves (so all T4 completers should have all four waves). The numbers cannot be reconciled, and the tables' N values (321, 244) add further inconsistency.
issues.quote: Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample.

issues.subcategory: Implausible/garbled CFA statistics
issues.description: The confirmatory factor analysis results are internally impossible. The four-factor model is reported with a chi-square of 862.05 on 269 df but RMSEA = .08 with CFI = .99 and TLI = .99 — a chi-square/df ratio of ~3.2 with that RMSEA is inconsistent with CFI/TLI of .99. More critically, the alternative models report degrees of freedom of 3, 2, and 1 (e.g., 'a one-factor model (1) = 8.02') which is impossible — a more constrained one-factor model must have MORE degrees of freedom than the four-factor model, not fewer. These appear to be chi-square difference values mislabeled, but as presented they are uninterpretable, and a one-factor model with RMSEA = .10 still showing CFI = .98 is implausible.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than a three-factor model wherein both incivility measures were set to load onto the same factor (3) = 82.52, RMSEA = .09, CFI = .98, TLI = .98)

issues.subcategory: Implausibly high inter-construct correlations / discriminant validity failure
issues.description: Table 1 shows correlations among purportedly distinct constructs that are extremely high (e.g., T1 Customer Incivility with T1 Compassion Fatigue r = .80; T1 Negative Emotions with T1 Compassion Fatigue r = .83; T4 Compassion Fatigue with T4 Enacted Incivility r = .94). Correlations of .85–.94 between supposedly distinct constructs (especially r = .94 between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility) suggest the measures are not discriminant and may reflect the same underlying factor or massive common method variance, directly contradicting the claimed CFA discriminant validity. The authors acknowledge 'some of the bivariate relationships are higher than convention' but do not adequately address that these magnitudes threaten the entire construct structure.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory regression coefficients between Tables 2 and 3
issues.description: The same paths are reported with materially different coefficients across tables without explanation. In Table 2, the path from T2 Customer Incivility to T3 Negative Emotions is B = .26, but in Table 3 (moderated model) the same path (main effect A) is B = .22. The path from T4 Compassion Fatigue to Enacted Incivility is B = .57 (p < .001) in Table 2 but B = .40 (p = ns, t = 1.74) in Table 3. The compassion fatigue→enacted incivility path being significant in one model and nonsignificant in another, with the main mediation hinging on this path, is a serious inconsistency. The body text reports yet another value (B = .23) in the relative importance analysis.
issues.quote: T4 Compassion Fatigue |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | .57*** | .17 | 3.35

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent reporting of key mediation coefficient
issues.description: Hypothesis 2's path d (negative emotions → compassion fatigue) is reported as B = .37 in the text and Table 2, but the direct relationship between experienced incivility and compassion fatigue is reported as B = .13. Meanwhile the supplemental relative importance analysis reports negative emotions B = .23 and compassion fatigue B = .23 predicting enacted incivility—values that do not match the B = .28 and B = .57 from Table 2 for the same predictors of enacted incivility. These inconsistencies across the text and tables for identical paths cannot be reconciled and prevent verification.
issues.quote: we regressed enacted incivility on predictors from this stage--experienced incivility (B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40), negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001), and compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001).

issues.subcategory: Single-item perception measure for key moderator
issues.description: Patient acuity, a central moderator, is operationalized as a single self-report item asking the percentage of patients perceived as 'severe.' This conflates perceived workload, illness severity, and emotional demand; cannot be assessed for reliability; and the authors concede it may not reflect actual acuity. Given that acuity is theorized as a 'task-related stressor' distinct from interpersonal incivility, a single perception-based percentage item is a weak operationalization that may actually capture general negative perceptions, threatening the moderation construct validity.
issues.quote: we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were “severe.”

issues.subcategory: Construct mismatch in compassion fatigue framing
issues.description: The manuscript states it examines 'the relationship between experiencing coworker incivility and experiencing a caregiving specific form of job burnout, compassion fatigue,' but the entire study concerns PATIENT (customer) incivility, not coworker incivility. This is either a serious conceptual slip or indicates the theoretical development was imported from a coworker-incivility framework, raising questions about whether the hypothesized mechanisms were correctly mapped to the customer-incivility context.
issues.quote: Within the current study, we look specifically at the relationship between experiencing coworker incivility and experiencing a caregiving specific form of job burnout, compassion fatigue.

issues.subcategory: Overreaching causal claims from correlational panel data
issues.description: The authors repeatedly claim their autoregressive design 'allows for stronger causal inferences' and describe 'trickle-down effects' and that incivility 'leads to' enacted incivility. While autoregressive cross-lagged models reduce some confounding, they do not establish causation, particularly with all variables self-reported, no manipulation, and the possibility of unmeasured time-varying confounders. The language throughout (e.g., 'leads to,' 'causal effects,' 'impacts future behaviors') overstates what observational panel data can support.
issues.quote: allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time

issues.subcategory: Partial vs. full mediation contradiction
issues.description: The Discussion states 'Our results support a partial mediation process,' but the hypotheses (H2 and H4) were framed as fully indirect ('is positively and indirectly related,' 'is indirect through'). The results also report a significant direct effect of incivility on compassion fatigue (B = .13, p < .001), confirming only partial mediation, which contradicts the hypothesis framing. This inconsistency between hypothesized full indirect effects and observed partial mediation is not reconciled.
issues.quote: Our results support a partial mediation process: in support of our hypotheses, experiencing incivility from patients was related to increased future incivility enactment towards patients indirectly

issues.subcategory: Mediation temporal ordering collapses required lags
issues.description: The serial mediation (incivility T2 → negative emotions T3 → compassion fatigue T4 → enacted incivility T4) requires four temporally ordered steps but only spans three waves, forcing compassion fatigue (T4) and enacted incivility (T4) to be measured concurrently. This means the final and most theoretically important link (compassion fatigue → enacted incivility) is cross-sectional, not lagged, undermining the claim of a temporally-ordered causal chain and the central 'over time' contribution for that path.
issues.quote: the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying each stage in the serial mediation process (a × b × d). As expected, Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients

issues.subcategory: Inadequate handling and reporting of missing acuity data
issues.description: Patient acuity had substantial missingness (reducing N from 321 to 244, ~24% loss) handled apparently via listwise deletion. The authors only report no demographic differences but provide no test of whether missingness related to the study variables themselves (e.g., incivility, negative emotions), no missing-data mechanism justification (MCAR/MAR), and no use of modern missing-data techniques (FIML/MI). Given the moderator analysis hinges on this reduced sample, this is a substantial threat.
issues.quote: Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response).

issues.subcategory: No selection/verification of inclusion criteria for full sample
issues.description: Inclusion in 'high-stakes/critical care' settings was verified by O*Net cross-check for only a random subsample of 20 participants, while the rest relied on self-report and self-selected response to a survey item. Given recruitment via open social media links and MTurk-style concerns (the study even excludes 21 for likely duplicate/collusion responses), the verification of the core eligibility criterion for the analytic sample is inadequate, threatening sample validity.
issues.quote: In addition, we reviewed the O*Net job descriptions for a randomly selected group of n = 20 participants.

issues.subcategory: Undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom / no preregistration
issues.description: The study reports no preregistration. There are numerous analytic choices that could have been made flexibly: which items were selected for shortened scales ('highest loading items'), choice of which waves serve as predictor vs. outcome, centering decisions, and the post-hoc 'supplemental analyses.' The labeling of H1 and H2 as 'replication hypotheses' after the fact, and exploratory supplemental analyses (relative importance), suggest flexibility that, without preregistration, inflates the risk of capitalizing on chance.
issues.quote: For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability

issues.subcategory: Enacted incivility floor effect and social desirability
issues.description: Enacted incivility toward patients is a self-reported admission of mistreating vulnerable patients, highly subject to social desirability and likely floor effects. Yet the manuscript reports a mean of 2.77 (SD = 1.21) on a 1–5 scale, implausibly high for self-reported rudeness toward patients, and 90% of pilot participants admitted engaging in these behaviors. Such high endorsement raises concerns that the items capture something other than genuine incivility enactment (e.g., perceived brusqueness under time pressure), threatening construct validity.
issues.quote: 90% of respondents indicated that they personally had engaged in these behaviors towards patients or their families.

issues.subcategory: Simple slopes / interaction reporting inconsistency
issues.description: The simple slope values reported in the text for H3 (low B = .13 p = .26; medium B = .22 p < .05; high B = .32 p < .001) match Table 3's simple slopes, but the main-effect coefficient for incivility→negative emotions in the moderated model (B = .22) equals the medium slope, and the interaction B = .34 with these slopes implies a specific spacing of the moderator that is not transparently documented (the moderator is a proportion 0–1, so ±1 SD = ±.28 around .52). The reported slope differences (.13 to .32 across the moderator range) and the claim of significant moderation rest on a sample (N=244) and a single-item moderator, and the low-acuity slope being nonsignificant is glossed as 'support.'
issues.quote: Simple slope analysis estimates at low (B = .13, SE = .12, p = .26, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.35]), medium (B = .22, SE = .09, p < .05, 95% CI [0.04, 0.40]), and high (B = .32, SE = .08, p < .001, 95% CI [0.17, 0.46]) levels of the moderator revealed support for Hypothesis 3.

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis 4 mechanism (b path) undefined/mislabeled
issues.description: Hypothesis 4's indirect effect is described as 'a × b × d', but earlier path 'b' is not clearly defined and the mediation chain labeling is inconsistent across the text. H2 uses 'a × d' (incivility→neg emotions→compassion fatigue), while H4 uses 'a × b × d' but also references negative emotions and compassion fatigue. The path labels (a, b, d) are never systematically defined, making it impossible to verify the serial mediation computation, and 'c' appears to be skipped entirely.
issues.quote: Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying each stage in the serial mediation process (a × b × d).

issues.subcategory: Sampling frame and self-selection limits generalizability
issues.description: Recruitment was via convenience methods (flyers at 3 local hospitals, personal networks, social media, MTurk pilot) with self-selected participation through open links. This non-probability, self-selecting sample of unknown response rate cannot support claims about nurses generally or 'service industries' broadly, yet the paper extends implications to 'employees in the service industries.' The acknowledgment of healthcare-specificity is present but the broader service-industry extrapolation in the conclusion overreaches.
issues.quote: Because incivility from customers is likely a common experience for employees in the service industries, providing resources that can help buffer the negative effects of experienced incivility is likely vital

issues.subcategory: Compassion fatigue scoring/combination not specified
issues.description: Compassion fatigue is described as comprising burnout and secondary trauma components ('experiencing either... or both'), but the analysis treats it as a single 13-item scale with one alpha (.96). It is not reported whether the two theorized components were combined into a composite, how, or whether they behaved differently. Given the conceptual emphasis on two distinct components, collapsing them without justification is a reporting and construct gap.
issues.quote: Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components, with employees experiencing compassion fatigue if they are experiencing either caregiving-related burnout or secondary trauma (or both of these simultaneously).

issues.subcategory: Misapplication of 'replication hypothesis' framing
issues.description: H1 is labeled a 'replication hypothesis' and the text repeatedly asserts the incivility–negative-emotion relationship is 'robust' and 'consistent across methodologies.' Framing a confirmatory test as a replication while drawing novel longitudinal conclusions is conceptually muddled, and treating well-established relationships as hypotheses to be 'supported' inflates the apparent confirmatory success rate of the study without adding new knowledge for those paths.
issues.quote: In this context, we propose the following replication hypothesis:

issues.subcategory: Attrition comparison statistics not reported
issues.description: The claim that T1-only responders were 'similar' to completers and 'within one standard deviation of the means' is asserted without any statistical test, effect sizes, or table. 'Within one standard deviation' is an extremely weak criterion (most observations fall within one SD by definition) and does not constitute evidence of non-differential attrition. This prevents evaluation of attrition bias.
issues.quote: had scale values on the key study constructs within one standard deviation of the means for the final sample of respondents who completed all four time periods – this suggests that the participants who did not complete all time periods were likely not substantially different

issues.subcategory: Implausible R-squared escalation
issues.description: The R² values escalate implausibly across the mediation chain: .14 for negative emotions, .62 for compassion fatigue, and .81 for enacted incivility (Table 2). An R² of .81 for enacted incivility is extraordinarily high for behavioral self-report outcomes and, combined with the near-collinear predictor correlations (r = .94 between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility), strongly suggests the predictors and outcome are not distinct constructs, inflating explained variance artifactually.

issues.subcategory: No controls for prior levels of mediators/outcome in reported equations
issues.description: Although the analytic strategy describes autoregressive control using T1, the reported regression tables (Tables 2 and 3) include only work hours as covariates and do not transparently show the autoregressive (T1) terms in the prediction equations for negative emotions (T3), compassion fatigue (T4), or enacted incivility (T4). Without explicitly controlling for prior levels of each mediator/outcome, the lagged 'effects' may be confounded by stable trait variance, contradicting the stated autoregressive approach.
issues.quote: the first wave was reserved for controlling for autoregressive effects, and the subsequent waves were included for hypothesis testing

issues.subcategory: Negative emotions scale content-construct mismatch
issues.description: The Negative Emotions Towards Patients measure uses only four emotions—aversion, disgust, anger, and fear. Fear toward patients is conceptually distinct from the anger/hostility emotions the stressor-emotion model links to CWB, and including fear may dilute or distort the affective mechanism. The selection of these four specific emotions, and exclusion of more directly relevant ones (e.g., frustration, contempt), is not justified relative to the theoretical model.
issues.quote: The scale items consisted of four negative emotions: (a) aversion, (b) disgust, (c) anger, (d) fear.

issues.subcategory: Monte Carlo / model details insufficient for replication
issues.description: The analytic description mixes references to many methods (Edwards & Lambert, Hayes PROCESS, Preacher et al., Monte Carlo via Selig & Preacher, MPlus model constraint) without specifying the actual estimated model, estimator for the structural model, how the autoregressive paths were specified, or how the moderated mediation was integrated with the autoregressive structure. This 'kitchen sink' citation of methods without a single coherent specified model prevents replication.
issues.quote: Next, we followed procedures described by Edwards and Lambert (2007), Hayes (2015, 2017), Preacher et al. (2007), and Selig and Preacher (2009) to estimate direct and indirect effects at each stage of the simple and moderated mediation models.

issues.subcategory: Citation/year inconsistencies undermining scholarly rigor
issues.description: Numerous citations are inconsistent or erroneous (e.g., 'Grandy et al., 2007' vs 'Grandey et al., 2007'; 'Guimetti' vs 'Giumetti'; 'Schilplzand' vs 'Schilpzand'; 'Penny' vs 'Penney'; 'Arnold & Walsh, 2005' in text vs 2015 in references; Hülsheger 2020 in text vs 2021 in references; R Core Team 2021 in text vs 2020 in references). While individually minor, the pattern indicates insufficient care that compounds concern about the data-reporting inconsistencies elsewhere.
issues.quote: Like incivility from other workplace sources (e.g., coworkers), incivility from customers is associated with increased negative affective responses (Torres et al., 2017).

issues.subcategory: Reverse causality between enacted and experienced incivility unaddressed in model
issues.description: The theoretical premise is reciprocal ('incivility begets incivility'), and prior cited work (Vahle-Hinz; Rosen) shows bidirectional effects, yet the tested model is unidirectional (experienced → enacted). Nurses who enact incivility may provoke patient incivility, creating reverse causation. The autoregressive model controls for stability but does not include cross-lagged reciprocal paths (enacted T-1 → experienced T), leaving a major confound to the directional claim unmodeled.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 4:  The positive relationship between experienced patient incivility and enacted incivility towards patients is indirect through negative emotions towards patients and compassion fatigue.

issues.subcategory: Supplemental relative importance contradicts main mediation conclusion
issues.description: The supplemental relative importance analysis finds experienced incivility uniquely accounts for 24.1% of variance in enacted incivility, yet in that same regression its coefficient is nonsignificant (B = -.03, p = .40) and even negative. Relative importance attributing 24% to a nonsignificant, negatively-signed predictor is internally contradictory and suggests suppression/multicollinearity effects that the authors interpret as substantive importance, misleading the reader.
issues.quote: The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.subcategory: Compensation and repeat-participation threat to data integrity
issues.description: The $5/wave incentive combined with open social-media/QR recruitment created incentives for repeat/fraudulent participation, as evidenced by the exclusion of 21 likely duplicate/collusion responses and 56 with inconsistent demographics. This raises concern that undetected fraudulent or careless responses remain in the analytic sample, particularly problematic for an online, unverified nursing sample, threatening the integrity of all results.
issues.quote: duplicate responses (identical content, syntax, and formatting) to open ended attention check questions as other participants (suggesting repeat survey participation and/or collusion) (n = 21)
